articles.summary: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion. The finding also challenges our current understanding of the relationship between erosion and the release of carbon dioxide, and suggests that geologists and atmospheric scientists…

articles.title: Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded
articles.summary: Earth is warming faster than ever recorded, with scientists detecting a major acceleration in global temperatures since around 2015. A new study reveals that the warming rate has surged to approximately 0.35°C per decade, nearly double the average pace observed from 1970 to 2015. After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

articles.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
articles.summary: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.

articles.title: Microplastic shape can influence viral disease severity in rainbow trout
articles.summary: The shape of microplastics can influence how deadly a viral infection can be for fish, according to new research from William & Mary's Virginia Institute of Marine Science (VIMS). The findings suggest that some forms of plastic pollution pose greater biological risks than others, offering scientists a potential path toward reducing the environmental impacts of microplastics.

articles.title: Faraway tectonic forces may have accelerated the Gulf of California rifting
articles.summary: When the Baja California peninsula broke from mainland Mexico nearly 12 million years ago, it gave rise to the Gulf of California. New research suggests that this process of continental rifting was greatly accelerated due to tectonic forces on the opposite side of the Pacific Ocean.

articles.title: A massive asteroid slammed into the North Sea and unleashed a 330-foot tsunami
articles.summary: A decades-long mystery beneath the North Sea has finally been solved. Scientists have confirmed that the Silverpit Crater, buried 700 meters below the seabed, was created when a 160-meter-wide asteroid struck Earth roughly 43 to 46 million years ago. The violent collision blasted a towering curtain of rock and water 1.5 kilometers into the air and triggered a tsunami more than 100 meters high.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden oxygen reservoir deep inside Earth
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that magma deep inside Earth can store surprising amounts of extra oxygen, potentially revealing a hidden contributor to our planet's oxygen-rich atmosphere. The findings suggest that ancient volcanic eruptions may have helped transform Earth's atmosphere billions of years ago, with implications for understanding life on other planets.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.

articles.summary: Nature Geoscience, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02124-9 Uncritical extrapolation of soil erosion models developed in the Global North to Global South settings for which they were not designed reflects and perpetuates neocolonial biases in geoscience. To build a more accurate and equitable understanding of land degradation, we must rethink erosion research.

articles.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.

articles.summary: Among Kepler and TESS's many surprising exoplanet discoveries are the ultra-short-period (USP) planets. These planets move very quickly and complete an orbit in less than 24 hours. Ancient astronomers thought that Mercury was so fast—it goes around the sun every 88 days—that they named it after the Roman god Mercury, who was the fast-traveling messenger of the gods. They couldn't have known how sluggish Mercury is…

articles.summary: A kerosene-based gel developed by Concordia researchers could make rocket and satellite fuels easier to store and control.

articles.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
articles.summary: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.

articles.title: Snowfall and clouds may slow East Antarctic ice loss in a warmer world
articles.summary: A new modeling study, published in the journal Nature Climate Change, suggests that the East Antarctic Ice Sheet may be more resilient to extreme long-term warming than previously estimated. Increased snowfall, greater cloud cover and changes in atmospheric circulation could partially offset ice loss—even under very high carbon dioxide concentrations.

articles.title: Waves alter Antarctic polynyas by breaking up surrounding sea ice
articles.summary: Polynyas are one of Antarctica's great counterintuitive features: recurring areas of open water surrounded by vast expanses of sea ice. These unusual environments are hot spots for sea-ice production, ocean–atmosphere exchange and biological productivity. They are commonly maintained by powerful winds that push newly formed ice away from the coast, repeatedly exposing the ocean to the freezing Antarctic atmosphere.

articles.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
articles.summary: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.

articles.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction

New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store…

articles.title: Using machine learning to build safer cities
articles.summary: In eThekwini, researchers have harnessed machine learning and satellite data to spot the city's most landslide-prone zones. A new study published in Scientific Reports has found that urban development activities, including road construction, property development and vegetation loss, are significantly increasing landslide susceptibility across parts of eThekwini.

articles.title: 40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
articles.summary: Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.

articles.summary: EMSN236 supported recovery planning in central Portugal following Storm Kristin by mapping ground instability, monitoring landslide activity and assessing soil erosion and susceptibility to future erosion using satellite observations.

articles.title: Gene therapy offers to beat hepatitis B virus by muting its DNA
